---
title: "A · Locating pixels — methods"
---

The problem: L2 swath products store a 2-D array of values plus 2-D arrays of pixel-centre
latitude and longitude. There is no grid, so "which pixel covers this point?" is a
nearest-neighbour search on the sphere, and "which pixels touch this polygon?" is a region
query. We compared six families of approaches on the same granules, targets and machine (4 vCPU
container), each in a fresh process.

## Targets and scenes

* **Single site**: a point in the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge, California (wetland /
  rice / orchard mosaic).
* **100 points**: uniformly random (seed 42) inside the area seen by all six scenes.
* **Polygons**: a 3 km square and a 10 km-radius circle centred on the site, and Colusa County
  (US Census 1:500k boundary, ~3000 km²).
* **Scenes** (2023-06-02/03): MODIS Aqua near nadir (2 stacked granules) and swath edge, MODIS Terra mid-swath,
  VIIRS NOAA-20 near nadir (2 granules), VIIRS SNPP swath edge, ECOSTRESS (one 5632 × 5400 scene).
  Full-resolution lat/lon come from the separate geolocation products (MOD03/MYD03, VNP03MOD/VJ103MOD,
  ECO_L1B_GEO). Note that the lat/lon inside MOD11_L2 are subsampled 5×5 — a common trap.

All point queries return the nearest pixel centre by **great-circle distance** and are
checked against brute force. Polygon queries return all pixel centres inside the polygon grown by
the largest pixel half-diagonal (3.5 km MODIS, 1.3 km VIIRS, 80 m ECOSTRESS); the exact
"does the footprint touch the polygon, and how much of it" step is Part B.

## The methods

| Method | Build | Point query | Polygon query |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Naive: full** | nothing | haversine to every pixel, `argmin` | `shapely.contains_xy` on every centre |
| **Naive: box** (`numpy.where`) | nothing | `|Δlat|, |Δlon|` box mask, then `argmin` inside it | bbox mask + `contains_xy` |
| **xarray `.sel(method="nearest")`** | – | **fails**: 2-D lat/lon are not indexed by default | – |
| **KD-tree** (scipy `cKDTree`, `pykdtree`) | tree on unit vectors (x, y, z) | nearest neighbour; chord distance is monotone in arc length, so no dateline/pole issues | ball query around the polygon centroid + `contains_xy` (pykdtree: k-NN with distance bound) |
| **xarray `NDPointIndex`** (+ [xoak](https://xoak.readthedocs.io/) adapters) | `ds.set_xindex(("lat","lon"), NDPointIndex, tree_adapter_cls=...)` | `ds.sel(lat=..., lon=..., method="nearest")` | not supported |
| **S2** (pys2index) | C++ `S2PointIndex` | nearest neighbour | no region API in the binding |
| **S2 sorted ids** | leaf cell id of every centre (vectorised port of the S2 Hilbert-curve code, validated against `s2sphere`), sorted | target cell at level *L* + 8 neighbours → `searchsorted` ranges → `argmin` | S2 covering of the polygon → id ranges → `contains_xy` |
| **H3 sorted ids** | `h3ronpy.coordinates_to_cells` at resolution *r*, sorted | `grid_disk(cell, 1)` → lookup → `argmin` | `polygon_to_cells(..., contain="overlap")` → lookup → `contains_xy` |
| **Analytic** | per-scan orbit state (a few kB) | predict (line, sample) from geometry, then search a small window of the real lat/lon | predict the polygon outline in (line, sample) space → read that window |

The S2 level / H3 resolution is chosen so that cells are at least as large as the largest pixel
(S2 level 10/11/15, H3 res 5/6/9 for MODIS/VIIRS/ECOSTRESS). The true nearest centre is then always
in the target cell or a direct neighbour.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
h3Edge = [1281256, 483056, 182512, 68979, 26071, 9854, 3724, 1406, 531, 201, 76, 29, 11, 4, 1.5, 0.6]
s2Edge = d3.range(0, 21).map(l => 7842000 * Math.pow(0.5, l) * 1.0)
viewof pix = Inputs.range([50, 6000], {value: 1000, step: 10, label: "largest pixel size (m)"})
pickH3 = h3Edge.findLastIndex(e => e * 1.0 >= pix)
pickS2 = s2Edge.findLastIndex(e => e >= pix)
```

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`**Index resolution for a pixel size.** For a sensor whose largest pixel is
**${pix} m**, choose H3 resolution **${pickH3}** (average edge ≈ ${Math.round(h3Edge[pickH3])} m) or S2 level
**${pickS2}** (average cell ≈ ${Math.round(s2Edge[pickS2])} m). Finer cells mean fewer candidate
pixels per lookup but more cells to visit for polygons; coarser cells mean more \`argmin\` work per point.`
```
:::

## The analytic method in detail

Every other method on this page *searches*: it compares the target against millions of pixel
centres, or against an index built from them. The analytic method instead *predicts* which line and
sample of the swath array can see the target, using only the spacecraft's position and orientation
(a few kB of metadata that ships with each granule) and a dozen instrument constants. This is
"inverse geolocation": the data producer's geolocation maps (line, sample) → (lat, lon); we go
backwards. Because a prediction can be off by a pixel or two, it ends by reading a small window of the
real latitude/longitude around the predicted pixel and taking the nearest pixel centre.

### Terms and coordinate systems

**ECEF** (Earth-Centred, Earth-Fixed) is a 3-D Cartesian coordinate system in metres. Its origin is
the Earth's centre of mass, Z points to the North Pole, X to latitude 0°/longitude 0°, and Y to
0°/90°E. The axes rotate with the Earth, so a point on the ground has fixed ECEF coordinates.
MODIS documentation calls the same system **ECR** (Earth-Centred Rotating). We convert the target's
latitude, longitude and height to ECEF on the WGS84 ellipsoid, because the satellite positions in
the files are already in ECEF.

![](figures/diagram_ecef.png){fig-alt="ECEF axes with the Earth's centre, a satellite S, a target T, and the line of sight from S to T." width=70%}

The other terms used below:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ECI / J2000** | Earth-Centred *Inertial*: like ECEF but the axes stay fixed relative to the stars rather than rotating with the Earth. The ISS attitude for ECOSTRESS is given in J2000; we convert it to ECEF with astropy (GCRS → ITRS: precession, nutation and Earth rotation). |
| **S**, **T** | ECEF position vectors of the satellite (from the granule's orbit data) and the target (from its lat/lon/height). |
| **Nadir** | The point straight below the satellite, and the "down" direction from it. |
| **Line of sight (LOS)**, **u** | The unit vector from the satellite to the target, **u** = (**T** − **S**) / \|**T** − **S**\|. |
| **Scan** | One sweep of the scan mirror (MODIS, ECOSTRESS) or rotating telescope (VIIRS) across the track. Each scan images *N*<sub>det</sub> lines at once, one per detector in a short along-track column. |
| **Detector *d*** | Which detector in that column, 0 … *N*<sub>det</sub> − 1. Together with the scan number *k*, it gives the array row: **line** = *k* · *N*<sub>det</sub> + *d*. |
| **Sample *j*** | The array column: the position along one scan, 0 … *N*<sub>samp</sub> − 1. |
| **Scan angle θ** | How far the LOS is tilted across the track away from nadir, measured at the satellite. It sets the sample. |
| **Along-track angle φ** | How far the LOS is tilted forwards or backwards along the track. It sets the detector. |
| **View zenith angle η** | The same LOS measured from the vertical *at the target*. Earth curvature makes η larger than θ (MODIS edge: θ = 55°, η ≈ 65°). |
| **Slant range *r*** | The distance from the satellite to the target. |
| **Roll, pitch, yaw** | Small rotations of the spacecraft about its along-track (x), cross-track (y) and nadir (z) axes. |
| **Quaternion** | Four numbers that encode a 3-D rotation, used here for the ISS orientation (body → J2000). |
| **Bow-tie overlap** | At wide scan angles, neighbouring scans' footprints grow and overlap (MODIS especially), so one target can be seen by two scans. |

: Terms used in the steps below. {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

### Step 1: the geometry of one scan

![](figures/diagram_scan_plane.png){fig-alt="Cross-section through the scan plane showing the satellite S at height h, nadir, a target T, scan angle theta at the satellite, view zenith eta at the target, and slant range r." width=80%}

![](figures/diagram_scans.png){fig-alt="Top view of three successive scans, each made of N_det detector lines, with sample index across the track and a target offset from the scan's centre line by phi minus phi0." width=85%}

The figures show the two angles that matter. Across the track, the mirror tilts the LOS by the scan
angle θ, and θ determines the sample *j*. Along the track, the detectors of one scan sit side by side, so a
target slightly ahead of or behind the centre of the detector array is seen by a different
detector. Its offset is the along-track angle φ, and φ determines the detector *d*.

### Step 2: a spacecraft reference frame

To measure θ and φ, **u** has to be expressed in axes attached to the spacecraft:
**x** along-track (direction of flight), **z** towards nadir, and **y** = **z** × **x** across the track.
Each scan has its own frame (a 3 × 3 rotation matrix whose columns are **x**, **y**, **z** in ECEF),
built from the granule's metadata:

* **MODIS** (`MOD03`/`MYD03`): the file provides this matrix for every scan (`T_inst2ECR`, instrument
  frame → ECR). No modelling needed.
* **VIIRS** (`VNP03MOD`/`VJ103MOD`): we build an *orbital frame* from the per-scan position
  (`orb_pos_ev_mid`) and velocity (`orb_vel_ev_mid`). **z** is the downward normal of the WGS84
  ellipsoid below the satellite (geodetic nadir). **x** is the *inertial* velocity, made perpendicular to **z**.
  The file's velocity is relative to the rotating Earth (ECEF). The spacecraft actually flies along its
  inertial velocity, which is that velocity plus the Earth's rotation, **v** + **ω** × **S** (figure,
  right). Without this correction the frame is yawed by up to ~3.5° and swath-edge pixels land tens of km
  away.
* **ECOSTRESS** (`ECO_L1B_ATT`): the ISS is not aligned with its orbit. It flies pitched ~7° and yawed a
  few degrees, so we use its measured orientation: attitude quaternions (body → J2000), converted to
  ECEF and interpolated to each scan's time. An orbital frame here would put swath-edge pixels hundreds of lines off.

For VIIRS and ECOSTRESS the frame is then rotated by a small calibrated pitch and yaw (below) that
absorb instrument mounting offsets.

![](figures/diagram_frames.png){fig-alt="Left: the spacecraft frame with x along-track, y cross-track and z to nadir. Right: inertial velocity as the sum of the Earth-fixed velocity and omega cross S, about 3.5 degrees apart." width=95%}

### Step 3: angles from the line of sight

Write **u** in that frame as (*u*<sub>x</sub>, *u*<sub>y</sub>, *u*<sub>z</sub>), its components along **x**, **y**, **z**. Then

* scan angle **θ = atan2(*u*<sub>y</sub>, *u*<sub>z</sub>)**: the tilt of the LOS from nadir within the
  cross-track plane (0 at nadir; MODIS reaches ±55°, VIIRS ±56°, ECOSTRESS ±25.5°);
* along-track angle **φ = asin(*u*<sub>x</sub>)**: the small tilt forwards/backwards (a few mrad).

### Step 4: the satellite moves during a scan

![](figures/diagram_timing.png){fig-alt="Satellite positions along the orbit at the times different scan angles are observed, spanning about 2.9 km for MODIS Aqua." width=95%}

The file stores one position per scan, valid at a reference time *t*<sub>scan</sub>: MODIS "EV centre
time", VIIRS `ev_mid_time`, and for ECOSTRESS the start time of the scan's first line. But the mirror
sweeps across the swath over a fraction of a second while the satellite moves at ~7 km/s. The sample at
scan angle θ is observed at

> *t* = *t*<sub>scan</sub> + *t*<sub>off</sub> + *s* · κ · θ

where κ (seconds per radian) is how long the LOS takes to rotate through one radian, *s* = ±1 is the
direction of the sweep, and *t*<sub>off</sub> is the time at which the LOS points to nadir (θ = 0),
measured from *t*<sub>scan</sub>. We move **S** to that time (**S** + **v** · (*t* − *t*<sub>scan</sub>))
and recompute θ and φ. Two iterations suffice.

### Step 5: angles → array indices

![](figures/diagram_index_maps.png){fig-alt="Left: sample index versus scan angle, linear for MODIS and piecewise for VIIRS. Middle: VIIRS native-to-aggregated sample mapping with 1:1, 2:1, 3:1 zones. Right: detector index versus along-track angle for MODIS." width=100%}

* **Sample.** Samples are evenly spaced in scan angle, α radians apart, so
  **j = j<sub>c</sub> + s · θ / α** (MODIS, ECOSTRESS), where *j*<sub>c</sub> is the sample at nadir.
  VIIRS applies the same formula to its 6304 *native* samples. To keep pixels from growing too fast,
  it then sums them on board: 3 native → 1 near nadir, 2 → 1 further out, 1 → 1 at the edges
  (640 × 1:1, 368 × 2:1, 1184 × 3:1, 368 × 2:1, 640 × 1:1 = 3200 output samples). We map the native
  index through these zones (middle panel).
* **Detector.** Detectors are δ radians apart along-track, centred on the angle φ<sub>0</sub>, so
  **d = d<sub>c</sub> + (φ − φ<sub>0</sub>) / δ**, where *d*<sub>c</sub> = (*N*<sub>det</sub> − 1)/2 is the middle detector.
  The line is *k* · *N*<sub>det</sub> + *d*.
* **Which scan?** For each target we first pick the scan *k* whose φ (measured from that scan's
  position) is closest to φ<sub>0</sub>, then evaluate it and its two neighbours. The target belongs to the
  scan where −0.5 ≤ *d* ≤ *N*<sub>det</sub> − 0.5. Under bow-tie overlap two scans qualify. The prediction uses the one
  where *d* is closest to the centre, and the refinement step searches both. A target is
  *outside the swath* if no scan qualifies or *j* falls outside 0 … *N*<sub>samp</sub> − 1.

### Step 6: refinement

![](figures/diagram_refine.png){fig-alt="Two overlapping scans as pixel grids, an analytic prediction marked with a cross, a window of plus or minus k pixels around it in each scan, and the nearest pixel centre." width=80%}

The prediction is a fractional (line, sample). We read a window of ±*k* lines and samples of the
real latitude/longitude around it, in every candidate scan, and keep the pixel whose centre is nearest
to the target. How large *k* must be is the question of the widget below.
Each window stays inside its own scan's lines: across a scan boundary, adjacent array rows can be
kilometres apart on the ground (or overlap), so the next scan gets its own window instead.

### The constants

What each constant means:

| Symbol | Meaning | Units |
|---|---|---|
| *N*<sub>det</sub> | detectors (lines) per scan: MODIS 10, VIIRS 16, ECOSTRESS 128 | – |
| *N*<sub>samp</sub> | samples per line: MODIS 1354, VIIRS 3200 (6304 native), ECOSTRESS 5400 | – |
| α | scan angle between neighbouring samples (VIIRS: native samples) | mrad |
| *j*<sub>c</sub> | sample index that looks at nadir (θ = 0) (VIIRS: native index) | sample |
| *s* | direction of the sweep: sign of d*j*/dθ (−1 for all three in these files) | – |
| δ | along-track angle between neighbouring detectors | mrad |
| *d*<sub>c</sub> | middle detector, (*N*<sub>det</sub> − 1)/2: 4.5, 7.5, 63.5 | detector |
| φ<sub>0</sub> | along-track angle of the detector-array centre (nominally 0) | mrad |
| κ | time the LOS takes to rotate one radian (1 / LOS rotation rate) | s/rad |
| *t*<sub>off</sub> | time of the nadir look minus the file's scan time *t*<sub>scan</sub> (nominally 0) | s |
| pitch, yaw | extra rotation of the VIIRS/ECOSTRESS frame for instrument mounting (MODIS: already in `T_inst2ECR`) | ° |

: Constants of the analytic model. {tbl-colwidths="[14,74,12]"}

Their values, from the documentation ("spec") and after calibration ("cal."):

| Platform | α | *j*<sub>c</sub> | δ | φ<sub>0</sub> | κ | *t*<sub>off</sub> | pitch | yaw |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MODIS spec | 1.418 | 676.5 | 1.418 | 0 | 0.235 | 0 | – | – |
| Terra cal. | 1.418 | 677.9 | 1.418 | −0.28 | 0.192 | −0.090 | – | – |
| Aqua cal. | 1.418 | 678.1 | 1.418 | −0.93 | 0.225 | −0.165 | – | – |
| VIIRS spec | 0.3104 | 3151.5 | 0.895 | 0 | 0.284 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| SNPP cal. | 0.3117 | 3153.2 | 0.895 | +1.42 | 0.259 | +0.755 | −0.44 | +0.02 |
| NOAA-20 cal. | 0.3104 | 3156.7 | 0.891 | −1.53 | 0.258 | −0.871 | +0.62 | +0.03 |
| ECOSTRESS spec | 0.1648 | 2699.5 | 0.172 | 0 | 0.188 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| ISS cal. | 0.1714 | 2701.4 | 0.185 | +0.02 | 0.139 | +0.138 | +0.30 | +0.09 |

: Units as in the table above. All calibrated values: [`results/analytic_models.json`](https://github.com/ashiklom/simon-code-research/blob/main/l2-swath-geolocation/results/analytic_models.json). {tbl-colwidths="[22,10,11,10,10,9,10,9,9]"}

Spec values come from the instrument documentation. MODIS: 1354 frames of 1.418 mrad over ±55°,
two-sided mirror at 20.3 rpm, so the LOS turns at 4.25 rad/s (MOD03 geolocation ATBD). VIIRS: 6304
native samples over ±56.06°, 1.7864 s per telescope revolution, 742 m detectors at 829 km (VIIRS
geolocation ATBD). ECOSTRESS: 5400 samples over ±25.5°, two-sided mirror at 25.4 rpm, 69 m detectors
at ~400 km (ECOSTRESS L1 ATBD). Roll is not fitted because a small roll does the same thing as a shift
of *j*<sub>c</sub>. For VIIRS, *t*<sub>off</sub> and pitch both move the prediction along-track and
partly trade off against each other. That is why the two VIIRS platforms have large values of opposite sign that
mostly cancel, so read them as a pair rather than as physical timing errors.

**Calibration and testing.** The documentation alone misses timing offsets and mounting angles. With
spec constants, MODIS needs a ±3 pixel window, VIIRS 6–14 and ECOSTRESS ±107. We therefore fit
*j*<sub>c</sub>, α, φ<sub>0</sub>, δ, κ, *t*<sub>off</sub> (and pitch/yaw) by least squares on one reference granule per
platform (June 2024, California), using 3000 of that granule's own pixel centres as truth. We then
**freeze** the constants and test them on 53 scenes: 6 regions (equatorial, Sahara, Siberia, Argentina,
near the dateline, California), ascending and descending passes, 2013 vs 2024 (before/after the Terra
and Aqua orbit lowering and drift), SNPP vs NOAA-20, and ECOSTRESS in 2019 and 2024 (different ISS
altitudes). The orbit itself is never assumed: each granule's own position, velocity and attitude are
used, which is why orbit drift does not matter. With the target's terrain height (from a DEM, or the
geolocation file's `height`), the frozen constants find the right pixel within ±1 (MODIS), ±2 (VIIRS)
and ±3 (ECOSTRESS) pixels in every scene. Assuming height 0 widens this to ±3/±9/±16, because a raised
target appears shifted outwards by about *h* · tan η (parallax).

### Why a window, and how big?

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sensorA = Inputs.radio(["MODIS", "VIIRS", "ECOSTRESS"], {value: "MODIS", label: "sensor"})
viewof thetaA = Inputs.range([0, 55], {value: 40, step: 0.5, label: "scan angle (°)"})
viewof terrain = Inputs.range([0, 3000], {value: 800, step: 50, label: "terrain height ignored (m)"})
cfgA = ({MODIS: {h: 705e3, a: 1.418e-3, max: 55}, VIIRS: {h: 829e3, a: 0.312e-3, max: 56}, ECOSTRESS: {h: 415e3, a: 0.171e-3, max: 25.5}})[sensorA]
geomA = {
  const R = 6371e3, th = Math.min(thetaA, cfgA.max) * Math.PI / 180, Rs = R + cfgA.h;
  const eta = Math.asin(Rs / R * Math.sin(th));
  const r = Rs * Math.cos(th) - Math.sqrt(R * R - Rs * Rs * Math.sin(th) ** 2);
  let agg = 1;
  if (sensorA === "VIIRS") agg = thetaA < 31.59 ? 3 : thetaA < 44.68 ? 2 : 1;
  const Ws = r * cfgA.a * agg / Math.cos(eta);
  const shift = terrain * Math.tan(eta);
  return {vza: eta * 180 / Math.PI, r, Ws, shift, px: shift / Ws};
}
```

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`At a scan angle of **${Math.min(thetaA, cfgA.max)}°** the view zenith angle is **${geomA.vza.toFixed(1)}°** and the
along-scan pixel is **${(geomA.Ws).toFixed(0)} m** wide. Predicting the pixel for a target at sea level when it
actually sits **${terrain} m** up shifts the line of sight by h·tan(VZA) = **${geomA.shift.toFixed(0)} m**, i.e.
**${geomA.px.toFixed(1)} pixels** along-scan. That parallax, not the orbit model, sets the search window when
no DEM is used — which is why ECOSTRESS (70 m pixels) needs a much larger window than MODIS without terrain heights.`
```
:::

## Benchmark protocol

* Each (scene, method) runs in a new process; geolocation is read once (timed separately as "load").
* Build: median of up to 3 runs (fewer if > 30 s total). Queries: median of up to 5 (single site), 3 (100 points, polygons).
* "Index MB": growth of the process RSS during the build (an upper bound on index size).
* Correctness: identical pixel to brute force (points), identical candidate set to the KD-tree (polygons).
* The analytic method runs **without** terrain heights, with the half-window found for that platform
  in the consistency test (Terra 3, Aqua 2, SNPP 9, NOAA-20 7, ISS 16 pixels), so it is
  exact by construction on those scenes; the pixels it reads are reported.

## Usability notes (xarray / xoak)

* `ds.sel(lat=..., lon=..., method="nearest")` on 2-D coordinates raises
  `ValueError: Could not automatically create PandasIndex` — xarray only indexes 1-D dimension coordinates.
* `xarray.indexes.NDPointIndex` (xarray ≥ 2025.07) is the supported route. Its **default adapter
  is a scipy KD-tree on raw (lat, lon) degrees**, i.e. Euclidean distance in degree space: wrong
  near the poles, across the dateline, and off by tens of metres at mid-latitudes (4 % of our
  100 points got the wrong MODIS pixel).
* xoak 0.2 now *only* supplies tree adapters for `NDPointIndex` (`SklearnGeoBallTreeAdapter` with the
  haversine metric, `S2PointTreeAdapter`); its own `ds.xoak.set_index/.sel` API is deprecated.
  With the right adapter, selection is one line and returns a Dataset with all variables; but there is
  no polygon/region query, no out-of-swath flag (the nearest pixel is always returned, however far),
  NaN coordinates are not allowed in the trees, and the index must be rebuilt for every granule.
